title: The Drowned Bell
pitch: Saltmere's storm-bell has been stolen and sunk. The tide is turning, the drowned are walking up the beach, and the only people who can fix it are the ones who broke it.
premise: For three hundred years the great bell of Saltmere has rung before every storm, and every time it rang the drowned dead stayed asleep beneath the bay. Three nights ago someone cut it from its tower and rowed it out past the breakwater. Tonight the worst storm in a generation is coming in, and lantern-light has been seen moving under the water. You are the five people in Saltmere with a reason to go out and bring it back: the one who stole it, the one who kept it, the one who sang for it, the one who owes the sea a debt, and the one who hears it ringing still.
setting: Generic coastal fishing town (Saltmere); drop into any setting with a sea.

posting.header: HANDS WANTED FOR A NIGHT'S WORK
posting.reward: The town's gratitude, and 300 gp from the harbourmaster

gmNotes: Act 1: the beach as the drowned rise (skirmish, rescue villagers). Act 2: the smugglers' cave where Rook delivered the bell — the buyer was a cultist of the Tidemother. Act 3: row out in the storm; the bell is tangled in a wreck 30 ft down, guarded by a drowned knight. Act 4: ring it before the tide turns — someone has to stay at the rope while the drowned climb the hull.

letters.title: A wet note from the Tern's bosun
letters.when: End of Act 1: once the beach is cleared, a drowned hand presses it into Marrow's palm
letters.text: Cap'n. Don't say it, you never could. We felt the hatchet go and we knew your arm by the weight of it. The Tern was already lost; the sea only wanted a count, and you gave her fewer than she meant to take. We have walked up this beach every storm for eleven years waiting for you to say our names. Say them tonight. But mind: when the bell rings true we wake for good, and the one who holds the rope goes down to keep us company. I'd sooner it were nobody. I'd sooner it were not you. Hob Tarrant, bosun.

letters.title: The buyer's receipt
letters.when: Act 2: in the smugglers' cave, when Rook opens the buyer's strongbox or shows the coin to anyone
letters.text: Thief. You were paid forty gold for the cutting and one coin for the rowing. The coin is the receipt. It remembers who carried the bell down, and tonight it will ask for payment. But a receipt can be passed on. Hold it to the rope when the bell rings and the sea will count you among her own, and the one who was owed will go free. Give it to the one who has been reaching for it, and she will be spared the walk down. You will not be asked twice. Be gentle with yourself in the choosing; the sea never is. The one in the sea-green coat.

letters.title: The old keeper's oilskin
letters.when: Act 3: found tied inside the drowned knight's gauntlet on the wreck
letters.text: To whoever keeps the bell after me. Three things I never put in the log. One: the bell is not hung to keep the dead asleep, but to keep a single debt unpaid. Two: if the bay ever gives you a drowned child who breathes on your slab, wash her, wrap her, and tell no one, for she belongs to the sea, and the sea will come for her when the bell goes under. Three: the keeper does not choose who stays at the rope. The rope chooses. I let a thief go once, too. Forgive yourself first. Keeper Aldous Thorne.

letters.title: The scrap from the black night
letters.when: Act 4: just before the ringing, when it slides out of Biddy's case on the hull
letters.text: You have carried this scrap since the black night in the boat and never read it by lamplight. Read it now. It is not a hymn. It is a lullaby, sung to a sleeper by the one who owns her, and the last verse is the only one that answers back. 'Sleep, you who counted the keel, let the rope go slack and kneel. One shall stay and one shall sing; neither is the sea's to bring.' It works in whoever's voice sings it, and it costs them the same. Choose the voice well.
